title: CELPIP General Listening — Practice Test 16
instructions: Listen to the audio for each part and answer the questions. Each audio plays once.

parts.title: Problem Solving
parts.description: A conversation in which one person has a problem and seeks help from another.

parts.title: Daily Life Conversation
parts.description: An everyday conversation between two people.

parts.title: Listening for Information
parts.description: An informational talk; listen for specific details.

parts.title: Discussion
parts.description: A discussion among people with different viewpoints.

parts.title: Viewpoints
parts.description: A longer talk presenting one speaker's opinion and reasons.

listeningScripts.title: A Bicycle Warranty Refused
listeningScripts.text: Customer: I brought a bike in three weeks ago with a cracked frame, and I've had an email saying the warranty claim has been refused. Shop: Let me find the ticket. What's the surname? Customer: Okonkwo. It's the grey commuter, bought in March. Shop: Right. The manufacturer's assessor has put it down as impact damage, and impact isn't covered. Warranty covers manufacturing defects. Customer: There hasn't been an impact. It gets ridden to work and back, and it's locked in a garage. Shop: Let me say what I can here. The assessor doesn't see the bike. They see the photographs we send. And the photographs we sent were the four the manufacturer asks for, which are all of the crack itself. Customer: So nobody has looked at whether the rest of the bike is marked. Shop: Exactly that. If a frame has been hit hard enough to crack, there is almost always something else — a scuffed pedal, a bent lever, paint off a dropout. If yours has none of that, then that is evidence, and it is evidence nobody has seen. Customer: The bike is undamaged apart from the crack. Shop: Then bring it back in and I'll photograph the whole thing and put in a reassessment. That is a different process from an appeal, and it's faster — ten days rather than six weeks. Customer: Is there a cost? Shop: Not for the reassessment. If it is refused again, an independent engineer's report is about two hundred dollars, and I'll be honest with you: I would only spend that if the reassessment comes back with a reason that doesn't match the bike. Customer: What do I need to bring? Shop: The bike and the original receipt. Not the email — I have that on the ticket already.

listeningScripts.title: Splitting a Holiday Rental
listeningScripts.text: A: So the house is two thousand four hundred for the week, and there are six of us. B: Four hundred each. That's fine. A: Except it isn't six equal rooms. There's a double with the ensuite, two twins, and a single that is essentially a cupboard with a window. B: Then whoever is in the cupboard shouldn't be paying four hundred. A: Agreed. What's fair? B: Weight it. The double pays four fifty a head, the twins four hundred, the single three hundred. A: That comes to twenty-seven hundred, not twenty-four. B: Then it's four twenty-five, three seventy-five and three hundred. Let me do it properly rather than in my head. A: Do that. The other thing is the car. Priya and Tom are flying in and the rest of us are driving. B: So they'll want a lift from the airport, and that's fifty minutes each way. A: I don't mind doing it. I do mind doing it twice, so they need to be on the same flight or take the bus. B: I'll tell them. And food. Are we doing a kitty, or splitting receipts at the end? A: Kitty. Every time we've split receipts somebody has ended up chasing forty dollars in November. B: Sixty each to start, and we top it up if it runs out.

listeningScripts.title: Pool Lane Swimming and Lessons
listeningScripts.text: Morning. This is the five-minute version for people who have just joined, and there is a laminated copy on the noticeboard by the changing rooms. Lanes first. There are three of them, and they go by speed, not by stroke. The near lane is slow, the middle is medium, the far lane is fast. The mistake people make is choosing the lane they would like to be in. Choose the one where you will not be overtaken. And if you are overtaken twice in a single length, move in a lane. Nobody minds that. Everybody minds the other thing. Circle swimming applies whenever there are three or more people in a lane: up the right-hand side, back along the left. With two of you, you can split the lane down the middle, but you have to agree it, and the way you agree it is by speaking, not by assuming. Lessons run in the far two lanes from four to six on weekdays, so the fast lane is not available then. That is the single most common complaint we get, and it is on the timetable. The pool closes for chemical checks from one to two on Wednesdays, and it is not a soft closure. You will be asked to get out. Kickboards and pull buoys are in the bins at the deep end, and they go back in the bins, not on the side. And please don't wear a watch that beeps. I know how petty that sounds. In a tiled room with water in it, one beeping watch is audible in every lane.

listeningScripts.title: Saskatchewan Rural Broadband Agreement
listeningScripts.text: Saskatchewan will extend high-speed internet to forty rural communities over three years, under an agreement announced this week. The cost is ninety-one million dollars, split between the province and the federal government. The work uses fibre for thirty-one of the communities, and fixed wireless for the remaining nine, where the distances make fibre uneconomic. Fixed wireless delivers lower speeds and is more affected by weather, and the province acknowledged as much, saying that the alternative for those nine communities was nothing at all for the foreseeable future. The target is fifty megabits down and ten up, which is the federal standard. The province says about eleven thousand households sit within the areas covered. A rural municipalities association welcomed the agreement but noted that it covers the connection to the community rather than to the individual property, and that the last stretch — the driveway, in effect — is where previous programmes have stalled. Construction begins next spring, with the first communities connected by the following winter.

listeningScripts.title: Replacing a Bus Route With On-Demand Minibuses
listeningScripts.text: Tanaka: Route 12 carries eleven passengers an hour across the day. A forty-seat bus, every thirty minutes, for eleven people. On-demand minibuses would cost about a third less and would get most people closer to their door. Byrne: Most people. Which ones are not in most? Tanaka: The ones without a smartphone, mainly. There is a phone line, but it books in fifteen-minute windows rather than instantly. Haddad: And that is the whole objection. The people still riding Route 12 at two in the afternoon are the people least likely to have the app. You would be moving to a system that works worst for the passengers you actually have. Tanaka: The phone line closes that gap. Haddad: It closes it for somebody who plans. It does not close it for somebody standing at a stop. Byrne: There is also the stop itself. A fixed route means a shelter, a timetable, and somewhere to stand. On-demand means standing at a kerb not knowing whether you are in the right place. Tanaka: We would keep twelve of the stops as designated pickup points, with the shelters. Byrne: Twelve of how many? Tanaka: Thirty-one. Haddad: Then say that in the consultation. Not most stops retained. Tanaka: That's fair. Twelve of thirty-one, and I will put the phone-line booking window in the same paragraph. Byrne: And run the two side by side for a season. If the minibuses work, the route empties on its own, and nobody has to be told they have lost a bus.

listeningScripts.title: Dropping Degree Requirements
listeningScripts.text: Several large employers, and a number of governments, have announced that they are removing degree requirements from jobs that do not need one. The announcements are easy to make. What I want to look at is what happens afterwards, because the follow-through has been poor, and the reasons for that are instructive. The case itself is straightforward, and I accept it. A degree requirement on a job that does not need a degree screens out a great many people who could do the work, and it screens them out in a patterned way — by income, by region, by who could afford three years. Removing it costs the employer almost nothing. Here is what the data then shows. In the year after these announcements, the share of hires without a degree moves very little. One large study put it at under four per cent of the affected roles. The requirement came off the advertisement and the hiring stayed the same. Why? Because the requirement was never doing the work people thought it was doing. It was a shortcut for the person reading two hundred applications on a Thursday afternoon. Take the line out of the advert and you have not given that person a replacement, so they apply the same shortcut informally — which is worse, because it is now invisible and nobody can audit it. What the employers who actually moved the number did was different. They changed what the first screen was: a skills task, a structured interview with fixed questions, a work sample. Something that takes the decision off the reader's impression. That costs real money, and it is why most firms stop at the announcement. So support it, and judge it on the number rather than the press release. When an employer says it has dropped degree requirements, the question worth asking is what replaced them.

questions.prompt: Why is the customer in the shop?
options: A bicycle bought in March has been recalled
A repair carried out three weeks ago has failed
A frame was damaged while the shop had it
A warranty claim on a cracked frame has been refused
questions.correctAnswer: A warranty claim on a cracked frame has been refused
questions.explanation: The customer brought the bike in three weeks ago with a cracked frame and has since had an email refusing the warranty claim.

questions.prompt: On what ground was the claim refused?
options: The bike was bought more than a year ago
The assessor recorded it as impact damage
The frame had been repaired before
No receipt was supplied with the claim
questions.correctAnswer: The assessor recorded it as impact damage
questions.explanation: The manufacturer's assessor put it down as impact damage, which the warranty does not cover — the warranty covers manufacturing defects.

questions.prompt: What does the shop say about the assessor?
options: They are employed by the shop rather than the manufacturer
They refuse most claims of this kind
They judge the claim from photographs rather than the bicycle
They inspected the bike while it was in the workshop
questions.correctAnswer: They judge the claim from photographs rather than the bicycle
questions.explanation: The assessor never sees the bike itself, only the photographs the shop sends — which is the opening the shop then works with.

questions.prompt: What did the four photographs show?
options: The crack itself
The whole bicycle from four angles
The pedals, levers and dropouts
The frame number and the receipt
questions.correctAnswer: The crack itself
questions.explanation: The four photographs the manufacturer asks for are all of the crack, which is why nothing else about the bike's condition reached the assessor.

questions.prompt: What would count as evidence in the customer's favour?
options: The number of miles the bike has covered
The date of purchase in March
The shop's own opinion of the crack
The absence of any other damage on the bicycle
questions.correctAnswer: The absence of any other damage on the bicycle
questions.explanation: The shop's argument is that a frame hit hard enough to crack almost always carries other marks — a scuffed pedal, a bent lever, paint off a dropout — so their absence is evidence nobody has yet seen.

questions.prompt: How does a reassessment differ from an appeal?
options: It is decided by the shop rather than the manufacturer
It can only be used once
It is faster, taking ten days rather than six weeks
It requires an engineer's report
questions.correctAnswer: It is faster, taking ten days rather than six weeks
questions.explanation: The shop distinguishes the two: a reassessment is a different process and takes ten days against six weeks for an appeal.

questions.prompt: What would an independent engineer's report cost?
options: About two hundred dollars
Nothing, if the reassessment fails
The same as the reassessment
It depends on the manufacturer's decision
questions.correctAnswer: About two hundred dollars
questions.explanation: The reassessment is free; an independent engineer's report, if it came to that, is about two hundred dollars.

questions.prompt: When would the shop think that report worth paying for?
options: Only if the frame is still under warranty
Only if the reassessment gives a reason that does not match the bike
Whenever a claim has been refused twice
If the customer intends to go to court
questions.correctAnswer: Only if the reassessment gives a reason that does not match the bike
questions.explanation: The shop is candid that the report is only worth two hundred dollars if the reassessment comes back with a reason that does not fit the bicycle in front of them.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with dividing the cost equally?
options: Not everyone is staying the full week
Two of the six are arriving by air
The rooms are not equivalent
The total has not been confirmed
questions.correctAnswer: The rooms are not equivalent
questions.explanation: A points out that six people does not mean six equal rooms: there is a double with an ensuite, two twins and a single barely larger than a cupboard.

questions.prompt: What does B propose instead?
options: Charging a different amount for each type of room
Drawing lots for the rooms
Asking the owner for a discount
Letting the single room go unused
questions.correctAnswer: Charging a different amount for each type of room
questions.explanation: B suggests weighting the price by room, with the double paying most and the single least.

questions.prompt: Why does B want to work the figures out again?
options: A disagreed with the amounts
The single room should pay nothing
The price of the house may change
The first attempt adds up to more than the rental costs
questions.correctAnswer: The first attempt adds up to more than the rental costs
questions.explanation: A notices that B's first weighting comes to twenty-seven hundred against a rental of twenty-four, so B revises it and says they will do it properly rather than in their head.

questions.prompt: What condition does A set on the airport lifts?
options: They must contribute to the fuel
Both arrivals must come on the same flight
They must arrive before the others
They must hire a car instead
questions.correctAnswer: Both arrivals must come on the same flight
questions.explanation: A is willing to make the fifty-minute run once but not twice, so Priya and Tom must be on the same flight or take the bus.

questions.prompt: Why do they choose a kitty rather than splitting receipts?
options: Splitting receipts has left somebody chasing money afterwards
A kitty is easier to divide evenly
Receipts are hard to keep on holiday
The kitty can be topped up
questions.correctAnswer: Splitting receipts has left somebody chasing money afterwards
questions.explanation: A's reason is experience: every time they have split receipts, somebody has ended up chasing forty dollars in November.

questions.prompt: How are the three lanes divided?
options: By stroke
By speed
By age group
By whether lessons are running
questions.correctAnswer: By speed
questions.explanation: The lanes go by speed and not by stroke: near is slow, middle is medium, far is fast.

questions.prompt: When should a swimmer move to a different lane?
options: Whenever the lane has three people in it
Whenever they are asked to by another swimmer
Only at the start of a session
After being overtaken twice in one length
questions.correctAnswer: After being overtaken twice in one length
questions.explanation: The rule given is to move in a lane after being overtaken twice in a single length — and the speaker notes nobody minds that, while everybody minds the alternative.

questions.prompt: When does circle swimming apply?
options: When there are three or more people in a lane
Whenever lessons are running
In the fast lane only
Whenever two swimmers cannot agree
questions.correctAnswer: When there are three or more people in a lane
questions.explanation: Circle swimming — up the right, back along the left — applies with three or more in a lane; with two, the lane may be split down the middle instead.

questions.prompt: How should two swimmers agree to split a lane?
options: By asking a lifeguard to confirm it
By starting at opposite ends
By saying so, rather than assuming it
By writing it on the board
questions.correctAnswer: By saying so, rather than assuming it
questions.explanation: Splitting the lane down the middle is allowed with two swimmers, but it has to be agreed, and the speaker is specific that agreeing means speaking rather than assuming.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker say is the most common complaint?
options: That the pool is too cold in the mornings
That the fast lane is unavailable between four and six
That equipment is left on the side
That lessons are too expensive
questions.correctAnswer: That the fast lane is unavailable between four and six
questions.explanation: Lessons occupy the far two lanes from four to six on weekdays, so the fast lane goes; the speaker calls this the single most common complaint and notes it is on the timetable.

questions.prompt: What happens at one o'clock on Wednesdays?
options: Lessons take over the whole pool
The equipment bins are restocked
The lanes are reorganised by speed
Swimmers are asked to leave the water for chemical checks
questions.correctAnswer: Swimmers are asked to leave the water for chemical checks
questions.explanation: The pool closes for chemical checks from one to two on Wednesdays, and the speaker stresses that it is not a soft closure — people are asked to get out.

questions.prompt: What is being extended?
options: High-speed internet, to forty rural communities
Mobile phone coverage, to forty rural communities
High-speed internet, to eleven thousand properties
A federal internet subsidy, to thirty-one communities
questions.correctAnswer: High-speed internet, to forty rural communities
questions.explanation: The agreement extends high-speed internet to forty rural communities over three years at a cost of ninety-one million dollars.

questions.prompt: What will be used where fibre is uneconomic?
options: Satellite, in nine of the communities
Fixed wireless, in thirty-one of the communities
Fixed wireless, in nine of the communities
Nothing, until a later programme
questions.correctAnswer: Fixed wireless, in nine of the communities
questions.explanation: Thirty-one communities get fibre and the remaining nine get fixed wireless, because the distances make fibre uneconomic there.

questions.prompt: What did the province acknowledge?
options: The cost is higher than first estimated
Fixed wireless is slower and more affected by weather
The three-year timetable may slip
Some communities will not be covered at all
questions.correctAnswer: Fixed wireless is slower and more affected by weather
questions.explanation: The province accepted that fixed wireless delivers lower speeds and is more weather-affected, while arguing that the alternative for those nine was nothing for the foreseeable future.

questions.prompt: What did the rural municipalities association point out?
options: The federal standard is too low to be useful
Fibre should have been used everywhere
Construction should begin before spring
The agreement reaches the community rather than each property
questions.correctAnswer: The agreement reaches the community rather than each property
questions.explanation: The association welcomed the agreement but noted it covers the connection to the community, not the individual property, and that the last stretch is where earlier programmes stalled.

questions.prompt: When are the first communities due to be connected?
options: Within three years of the announcement
By next spring
By the winter after construction starts
Once all forty are under construction
questions.correctAnswer: By the winter after construction starts
questions.explanation: Construction begins next spring, and the first communities are due to be connected by the following winter.

questions.prompt: What does Tanaka say about Route 12?
options: It runs every fifteen minutes
It costs a third more than it did
It carries eleven passengers an hour
It is the least used of thirty-one routes
questions.correctAnswer: It carries eleven passengers an hour
questions.explanation: Tanaka opens with the usage figure: eleven passengers an hour, carried by a forty-seat bus every thirty minutes.

questions.prompt: Who does Tanaka admit would be worse off?
options: People living furthest from the route
People without a smartphone
People travelling in the early morning
People who cannot walk to a shelter
questions.correctAnswer: People without a smartphone
questions.explanation: Pressed by Byrne on who is left out of most people, Tanaka names those without a smartphone, for whom there is only the phone line.

questions.prompt: What can the phone line not do?
options: Take bookings outside office hours
Reach the designated pickup points
Be used more than once a day
Book a journey instantly
questions.correctAnswer: Book a journey instantly
questions.explanation: The phone line exists but books in fifteen-minute windows rather than instantly, which is the gap Haddad presses on.

questions.prompt: What is Haddad's central objection?
options: The new system works worst for the passengers the route actually has
The saving has been calculated wrongly
Minibuses are less comfortable than buses
Drivers would lose their jobs
questions.correctAnswer: The new system works worst for the passengers the route actually has
questions.explanation: Haddad's argument is that the people still riding at two in the afternoon are the least likely to have the app, so the change works worst for exactly the passengers the route carries.

questions.prompt: What separate point does Byrne raise?
options: Minibus drivers need different training
Thirty-minute gaps are already too long
A fixed route provides a shelter and somewhere to stand
A phone line costs more to run than an app
questions.correctAnswer: A fixed route provides a shelter and somewhere to stand
questions.explanation: Byrne turns to the stop itself: a fixed route means a shelter, a timetable and a place to stand, while on-demand means waiting at a kerb unsure of being in the right place.

questions.prompt: How many stops would be kept?
options: Twelve of thirty-one
Twelve of forty
Thirty-one of forty
All of them, without shelters
questions.correctAnswer: Twelve of thirty-one
questions.explanation: Tanaka would keep twelve stops as designated pickup points with shelters, and confirms under Byrne's question that the total is thirty-one.

questions.prompt: What does Haddad ask Tanaka to do?
options: Delay the consultation until spring
Keep more of the stops
Consult the drivers separately
State the figure plainly in the consultation
questions.correctAnswer: State the figure plainly in the consultation
questions.explanation: Haddad asks that the consultation say twelve of thirty-one rather than most stops retained, and Tanaka agrees, adding the phone-line booking window to the same paragraph.

questions.prompt: What does Byrne propose at the end?
options: Trialling the minibuses on a different route
Running the bus and the minibuses together for a season
Keeping the bus until the app is improved
Putting the decision to a passenger vote
questions.correctAnswer: Running the bus and the minibuses together for a season
questions.explanation: Byrne's suggestion is to run the two side by side for a season, so that if the minibuses work the route empties on its own and nobody is told they have lost a bus.

questions.prompt: What have these employers announced?
options: That degree requirements are being removed from jobs that do not need one
That they will pay for employees' degrees
That degrees will count for less than experience
That they will hire a fixed share of non-graduates
questions.correctAnswer: That degree requirements are being removed from jobs that do not need one
questions.explanation: The announcements remove degree requirements from roles that do not need a degree, and the speaker notes such announcements are easy to make.

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker accept the case for it?
options: Degrees have become less rigorous over time
Employers cannot verify degrees reliably
Graduates are in short supply
The requirement screens out capable people along lines of income and region
questions.correctAnswer: The requirement screens out capable people along lines of income and region
questions.explanation: A degree requirement on a job that does not need one screens out many people who could do the work, in a patterned way — by income, by region, by who could afford three years.

questions.prompt: What does the data show in the year afterwards?
options: Applications rise sharply but hires fall
The share of hires without a degree barely changes
Non-graduate hiring roughly doubles
Employers quietly reinstate the requirement
questions.correctAnswer: The share of hires without a degree barely changes
questions.explanation: One large study put the movement at under four per cent of the affected roles: the requirement came off the advertisement and the hiring stayed the same.

questions.prompt: Why does removing the line change so little?
options: Candidates without degrees do not apply
Managers are not told the rule has changed
It was a shortcut for whoever reads the applications
The requirement remains in the job description
questions.correctAnswer: It was a shortcut for whoever reads the applications
questions.explanation: The requirement was a shortcut for the person reading two hundred applications on a Thursday afternoon, and removing the line gives that person no replacement for it.

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker say the informal version is worse?
options: It cannot be seen or audited
It is applied to more roles than before
It takes longer to reach a decision
It is harder for candidates to challenge in law
questions.correctAnswer: It cannot be seen or audited
questions.explanation: Applied informally the same shortcut is invisible and nobody can audit it, which the speaker considers worse than the written requirement it replaced.

questions.prompt: What did the employers who moved the number do differently?
options: They advertised the roles more widely
They set a target for non-graduate hires
They replaced the first screen with a task or a structured interview
They trained the people reading applications
questions.correctAnswer: They replaced the first screen with a task or a structured interview
questions.explanation: Those employers changed what the first screen was — a skills task, a structured interview with fixed questions, a work sample — anything taking the decision off the reader's impression, which costs real money.
